title: Tav (Shabbat 104a)
hook: emet, truth, uses the first, middle and last letters: truth spans everything

segments.voice: Yesterday, shin, the letter on the doorpost. Your line was shin on the door. Did your hand find the frame on the way out? Today, the last letter of the alef-bet. Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

Write the Hebrew word for a lie. Sheker. Three letters: shin, kuf, resh. Now look where they sit in the alef-bet. Kuf, resh, shin: three neighbors, right next to each other near the end, crowded together. Now write the word for truth. Emet. Alef, mem, tav. Alef stands at the very start of the alphabet. Tav stands at the very end. Mem stands between them. To spell the truth, you have to reach across the whole thing. The rabbis noticed this, and they didn't think it was an accident. Today, the letter that finishes the word, and the alef-bet.
screen: `SHEKER: THREE NEIGHBORS.` → `EMET: ALEF, MEM, TAV.` → `ACROSS THE WHOLE ALEF-BET.`

segments.voice: Tav. It makes a t sound, it's the last of the letters, and in the Talmud, tractate Shabbat, the rabbis read the end of the alef-bet like a parable. Four readings. First, the span. Emet starts with the first letter, passes through the middle, and ends with the last. Truth, the reading goes, has to be true at the beginning, true in the middle, and true at the end. A story that's honest only at the start isn't emet. Second, the crowd. The letters of sheker huddle together in one corner of the alphabet. The Talmud asks why, and answers: falsehood is easy to come by, and truth is hard to find. Lies are close at hand. Truth takes a reach. Third, the feet. The rabbis look at the shapes too. The letters of sheker, they say, each stand on a single leg. The letters of emet stand on broad bases, like bricks. The Talmud's line, put simply: truth stands, and falsehood does not stand. A lie needs propping up. Truth can bear weight. Fourth, the seal. Elsewhere in the same tractate, the Talmud says the seal of the Holy One is emet, truth. A seal is the mark at the end of a letter that says who it's from. Tav, the last letter, is where the seal goes. So the alef-bet ends with a letter that finishes the word for truth. The run of letters that began with a silent alef closes here, and the rabbis put truth across the whole span between them.
screen: `EMET: FIRST, MIDDLE, LAST.` · `SHEKER: NEIGHBORS IN A CORNER.` · `TRUTH STANDS; FALSEHOOD DOES NOT.` · `THE SEAL OF THE HOLY ONE IS TRUTH.` · then, large: `TRUTH FROM ALEF TO TAV.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell one truth. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small place where you've been leaning on a lie. Not a scandal. An I'm fine that isn't, a yes you didn't mean, a story you've been telling yourself. Notice how much effort it takes to keep it standing on one leg. Then find the true sentence, the one that could stand on its own feet. Say it silently to yourself first. Decide who needs to hear it, and when. If you pray, you can ask for courage. The bell holds the time.
Tav. The last letter of the alef-bet, the end of emet, truth, and in the Talmud's words, the seal of the Holy One. Today's word.
Your line: truth from alef to tav. Today, say the true sentence you found to the person who needs it, start to finish. Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Jewish learners study the letters of emet and sheker through the Talmud's teaching in Shabbat 104a; the word emet is also said in daily prayer right after the Shema.

original.note: Hebrew: truth — alef, mem, tav: the first letter, a middle one, and the last.

trapdoor: what you thought: tav is just the letter t at the end.
what it means: tav finishes emet, truth, which spans the alef-bet from first letter to last.
what a scholar hears: Shabbat 104a on sheker's crowded, one-legged letters and emet's firm ones; Shabbat 55a, the seal of the Holy One is emet.

notes: Shabbat 104a and 55a paraphrased throughout; no quotation marks. Confirm the paraphrases (sheker's letters close together, falsehood common and truth rare; one leg vs. firm base; truth stands, falsehood does not).

The 'first, middle, last' reading of emet is from the index; in the classical sources it is most explicit in the Jerusalem Talmud (Sanhedrin 1:1) and Genesis Rabbah 81. Mem is the middle letter only if the five final forms are counted (27 letters); the script says only that mem 'stands between them'. Confirm.
'Twenty-two days of letters that began with a silent alef' was cut to avoid a count; the line now says the letters 'began with a silent alef'. Check the final wording.
howItsDone: 'emet' said right after the Shema (emet v'yatziv / emet ve'emunah). Confirm phrasing.

Editor: the one-leg/broad-base point is now attributed to the rabbis ('they say') rather than stated as a description of the letterforms ('comes to a point at the bottom' was not accurate for every letter); added Shabbat 104a's brick image; varied the four-ways signpost.
